en: The Sūtra on the Dharma-Gate of Great Purity, translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus.
The assembly was gathered together: five hundred bhikṣus and eight thousand bodhisattvas. All were great sages who had attained dhāraṇīs and possessed immeasurable eloquence.

They had established and distinguished noble wisdom, understood the three gates of liberation, and were unimpeded in their wisdom regarding the three periods of time. They had attained samādhi that could not be shifted and were fully endowed with the ten powers and the fearlessnesses.

At that time, in the great city of Rājagṛha, there was a woman of loose conduct named Jyotīrasā, who was upright and exquisite, such that all who saw her were filled with joy; her physical form was pure and her majesty radiant like a flower, her body naturally the color of purple-polished gold as a reward for the roots of virtue she had cultivated in former lives.

Whether he was traveling, dwelling, lying down, sleeping, standing, sitting, rising, or walking in meditation, the ground upon which he moved manifested as a transformation identical to his own body. Even if he wore dyed silks, his garments would naturally turn into the color of gold, such that countless people could not help but revere him.
Those who beheld this woman could never tire of gazing upon her; her speech was neither coarse but gentle, harmonious, and beautiful, and her countenance was radiant, free from any sign of decay.

Within the great city of Rājagṛha, the sons of kings, crown princes, ministers, elders, and householders all gave rise to greedy and affectionate hearts, desiring to see her. Wherever she wandered—whether in gardens, by riversides, through streets and alleys, or among the trees—they would immediately follow her. Countless men and women, both old and young, all pursued her from behind, wishing to observe her.

At that time, on another day, the noble woman Jyotīrasā, together with the son of the householder Bhaya-bhīru, purchased fine goods to present as gifts. Having prepared exquisite delicacies, they proceeded to the Udyāna park. They traveled in a carriage drawn by four horses, adorned with banners, parasols, precious gems, and moon-like pearls, and decorated with purple gold. They spread out fine seats and carried various incenses and *campaka* flowers. Accompanied by female musicians, they went to the Udyāna park to enjoy themselves; their voices harmonized in song, and the sounds of drums and music led the way, while the implements of their offerings followed behind in a procession, which an incalculable number of people pursued to watch.

Mañjuśrī—whose name was translated into the Jin language as Pǔshǒu Tóngzhēn (Universal Chief Youth)—then emerged from his chamber, constantly giving rise to great compassion and pity for all living beings:

"What person might I exhort and transform so that they may set their minds upon the Mahāyāna, and through the three kinds of dharmas cause the wisdom of the Way to flourish—the transformation of supernatural powers, the transformation of preaching the Dharma, and the transformation of instruction—thereby guiding and benefiting them so they enter the discipline?"

At that time, Mañjuśrī saw the noble lady Jyotirindrayaśas together with the merchant’s son Bhayadatta, traveling in a carriage toward the pleasure grove; he knew the roots of the girl's past conduct and her virtuous merits from former lives.
"I shall manifest a transformation for him and preach the Dharma to him, ensuring that he attains understanding and penetration.

At that moment, Mañjuśrī transformed his body into that of a youth, whose countenance was exquisitely beautiful and surpassed that of the gods; all who saw him were filled with joy and could not help but revere him. His radiant and majestic appearance eclipsed the light of the sun and moon, and he appeared among humans clad in attire suited to his form.
The radiance of his robes illuminated forty *li*, and he manifested his body as if he were interested in something.
Once Mañjuśrī had finished adorning himself with his robes, he observed the path where the Licchavi girl wandered and soon stood before her on that very road.

Just as he stood before him, the chariot and horse of the elder’s son, as well as the carriage, garments, and ornaments of Suvarṇaprabhāśrī, were instantly eclipsed and ceased to appear; their radiance was utterly extinguished, like a mass of ink placed beside a bright pearl.

At that time, Suvarṇottamaprabhāśrī, the daughter of King Viḍoṭṭaka, beheld Mañjuśrī; his countenance was magnificent and exquisite like that of a celestial son, his body’s radiance was brilliant and beyond compare, his complexion was pleasing and lustrous, and his garments were extraordinary, with a dazzling brilliance emanating from his person.
Having seen this, he examined himself and did not consider it strange; coveting their clothing and attire, he thought to himself:
"I now wish to leave this son of the elder, step down from my carriage, and depart, so that I may enjoy myself together with these people."
"Furthermore, I vow that my own body shall obtain such clothing, appearance, and radiance.
As soon as she had thought this, Mañjuśrī established his majestic spiritual power, causing the Heavenly King Śikṣāsamudgata to transform himself into a man and say to the woman:
"Stop, stop! Do not speak thus!"
Why would one give rise to such a mind of indolence?
For what reason?
Because a person such as this does not set their will upon sensual desires.
The woman asked,
"For what reason?
The Deva King Śāntamati replied:
"This one is named the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī.
The girl asked again:
"For what reason is he designated by the title 'Bodhisattva'?"
Is he a deva-king?
Or is he a nāga, a yakṣa, a gandharva, a garuḍa, a kiṃnara, a mahoraga, a Śakra, a Brahmā, or one of the four heavenly kings?
Sīti replied, "If you wish to know who she is, she is neither a deva, nor a nāga, nor a spirit; nor is she Śakra or Brahmā.
She is called a Bodhisattva."
Furthermore, they are able to fulfill the wishes of all people; seeing that sentient beings have things they seek, they do not oppose their intentions, and are therefore called Bodhisattvas.
The woman thought to herself,
"According to what I have heard, he will surely give me exquisite garments.
She immediately alighted from her carriage and went to him, saying:
“O Benevolent One!
I pray that you would graciously bestow this robe upon me. Mañjuśrī replied:
"Sister! If you can resolve to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path, only then will I bestow this robe upon you.
The woman said:
"Yes, indeed.
What is meant by the Way?
He replied:
"If you wish to know, you yourself are the Way.
The woman asked, "How so?"
Mañjuśrī! If you do not extensively expound and analyze the meaning, I shall not understand it.
What is meant by "my own body is itself the Way"?
At that time, Jyotīrasa spoke in verse:
“Mañjuśrī, I pray you grant me this robe as a gift; only then shall I know that your noble mind is set upon the vast path of the Buddha.”
"Just as when the heavens do not rain and there has been a drought for a long time, one who is greedy and stingy is not a true bodhisattva.
At that time, Mañjuśrī spoke in verse:
"If this girl were able to give rise to the aspiration for the Way, then I would indeed—"
Generously bestowing robes as gifts;
if one possesses a firm mind and abides in the aspiration for the Way, all in the heavens and the world shall pay homage to them.
Jyotīrasa asked again in verse:
"What is the meaning of that which is called 'the Way'?
Who is it that teaches it? And who is it that attains the Way?"
"Regarding your aspiration for the study of the scriptures, what should you practice?
How can you attain the Buddha-way and transform those who have not yet awakened? Mañjuśrī replied:

"Sister! You should know that there is a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Śākyamuni, who is currently present preaching the Dharma, manifesting the equality of the body, and practicing the Way with universal equanimity."
"What do you think, sister?
Is it not from oneself that the aggregates, the elements, and the sense bases arise?
Hearing these words, the woman, through the power of her past virtues and the roots of merit accumulated by her former good deeds, attained the light of the Dharma and immediately replied:
"So it is, so it is! It is truly as you have said.
It is because of this body of mine that the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas) arise."
“Sister, what do you think?
Does form have any thought or any cognition?
The woman replied:
"No," Mañjuśrī replied, "Sister,
you should also know that the Way is without thought and without discrimination."
For this reason, form is equal and the Way is also equal.
Therefore I say this: "You yourself are the Way.
Sister, what do you think?
“Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness such that they have something to be mindful of,
or something to be distinguished? The woman replied, “No.”
Mañjuśrī replied:
“The Way is also without thought and without discrimination;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise equal, and the Way is also equal. Therefore, it is said: ‘You yourself are the Way.’”
"Sister, what do you think?
Can form be seen within, without, or in between?
Can blue, red, yellow, white, black, purple, or crimson be found in some particular place or direction?"
The woman replied,
“No. Mañjuśrī said in response:
“The Way, moreover, is without sight; it has no interior, no exterior, and no middle;
it possesses neither the hue of purple nor crimson, nor does it belong to any particular place or direction.”
Since form is already equal, the Path is likewise equal; therefore, this statement is made: "You yourself are the Path.
Sister, what do you think?
Can feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness be seen within, without, in between, or as having the appearance of the five colors in any particular direction?
The woman replied, “No. Mañjuśrī responded:
“The Way is also like this:
it does not abide within, without, or in between; it is not among the five colors; it has neither ‘that’ nor ‘this,’ nor does it have any spatial direction.”
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise equal, and the Path is also equal; therefore, it is said: "You yourself are the Path.
If the five aggregates are like an illusion, false, and inverted, arising from such causes, then the Path is also like an illusion, being merely a provisional designation based on sound.
Illusion is equality; the five aggregates are equality.
Since illusion is already equality, the Path is also equality; therefore, this statement is made: "You yourself are the Path."
The five aggregates are like a dream, having neither beginning nor end; the Way is also like a dream, fundamentally having no location.
Since the dream is characterized by equality, the Way is also equal; therefore, this statement is made: "You yourself are the Way."

When one calculates the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), they are like a mirage; the karma of delusion arises from falsehood. The Way is like a mirage—a matter of natural law—having neither creator nor retribution. Therefore, the mirage and the five aggregates are equal.
Since wild horses are already equal and the Path is likewise equal, it is for this reason that these words are spoken: "You yourself are the Path.
The five aggregates are like reflections; as reflections have no substantial existence, the Path—like a reflection—also has no substantial existence.
Thus, the reflection and the five aggregates are equal.
The mirror-image is equal, and the Path is also equal; therefore, this statement is made: "You yourself are the Path.
The five aggregates are merely provisional names for conditioned formations, and the Path is likewise merely a provisional name for the Path.
"The five aggregates are equal, and the Path is also equal; therefore, this statement was made:
'You are the Path. Mañjuśrī said:
"Listen further!"
The five aggregates have no creator, and the Way likewise has no creator;
the aggregates have no inherent nature, and the Way has no inherent nature;
the aggregates have nothing that exists, and the Way has nothing that arises.
The five aggregates are impermanent, and the Way brings clear understanding of impermanence;
the five aggregates lack peace, and the Way explains the meaning of suffering;
the five aggregates are empty and non-existent, and the Way brings thorough realization of emptiness.
The five aggregates are without self; to thoroughly understand the meaning of selflessness is the Way.
The various aggregates are quiescent; to thoroughly understand their tranquility is the Way.
The various aggregates are without reception; to thoroughly understand the meaning of non-reception is the Way.
The aggregates have no abiding and no attachment; this non-abiding and non-attachment is the Way.
The aggregates have no coming and no going; this non-coming and non-going is the Way.

Those who possess the five aggregates calculate the noble Dharma as being merely provisional sounds and words called "noble ones," yet within the Way they speak of them as friends; their speech is itself non-speech.

The five aggregates are entirely non-existent; fundamentally, they are all pure. The Tathāgata, having thus fully realized this fundamental purity, attained perfect enlightenment; therefore, it is called the Way (*mārga*).
For this reason, the five aggregates are fundamentally pure, and the Way is also fundamentally pure;
because the Way is pure, all phenomena (*dharmas*) are fundamentally pure.

"Now, Elder Sister, the aggregates (*skandhas*) are fundamentally pure; the Way of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, is also fundamentally pure. All things are fundamentally pure and are likewise spontaneous (*svabhāva*). The five aggregates of sentient beings are fundamentally pure in the same way; therefore, it is said: 'You yourself are the Way.'"
Having thoroughly understood the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), one then realizes that the Way is the Way of all Buddhas.
Furthermore, as for the Buddhas, they do not achieve the Buddha-way apart from the five aggregates.
The Way is not separate from the aggregates; it is through awakening to and fully comprehending the five aggregates that one is designated a Buddha.
"Therefore, Sister!
You should form this contemplation:
all sentient beings abide within the Path, and the Path also abides within all sentient beings; the Path is beyond words and conditions."
Therefore, this statement was made: "You yourself are the Way.
From that notion of a self, four kinds [of views] arise. What are these four?
These are earth, water, fire, and wind.
As for the element of earth, it is without self, without person, without life-span, and without vitality.
Being equal to the element of earth, the Way is likewise equal; fundamentally there is nothing received, and thus it is called equality.
The element of water is also equal, and the Way is its ultimate consummation; from beginning to end, it is spontaneous.
The element of fire is impartial, and the Way is its ultimate consummation; from beginning to end, it is without flaw.
The element of wind is equal; it is the beginning and end of the Way, yet nothing is seen therein.
Sister, you wish to know: as for the element of earth, it is by means of this very element that the Tathāgata attains enlightenment.
The element of water, the element of fire, and the element of wind—the lineage of the Tathāgata is likewise so; by means of these one attains the Way.
By thoroughly understanding the element of earth, as well as the elements of water, fire, and wind, one becomes a Buddha. Therefore, this meaning is taught: "You yourself are the Way."

The various elements of earth, water, fire, and wind are all without conceptualization; because one can remain free from such conceptualization regarding these four great elements, it is called the Way. For this reason, I say that you are the Way.
"Because of the self, there is then the eye; the ear, nose, mouth, body, and mind are likewise so.
The eye is empty; when one understands that the eye is naturally empty through discernment, this is the Way."
The ear, nose, mouth, body, and mind are likewise thus: when the mind is empty, and one understands that it is naturally empty, this is the Way.
When the eye is empty, it does not seek forms; when form is naturally empty, this is the Way.
The ear, nose, mouth, body, and mind are likewise so. When the mind is empty, it no longer seeks; all phenomena are without attachment. When phenomena are naturally empty, this is the Way.
The eye does not receive forms; the Way is likewise.
The eye has no forms, and the six sense-faculties are also thus, all being without that which is received.
Furthermore, when one calculates the nature of the Way, it is devoid of mental phenomena.
It is thus, Sister!
That eye-consciousness element does not abide within the form element;
neither the eye-consciousness nor the form element abides in the Path.

The auditory consciousness element, the olfactory consciousness element, the gustatory consciousness element, the tactile consciousness element, and the mental consciousness element do not abide in the dharma-realm; the Path, likewise, does not abide.
The mental factors and the element of consciousness—within the Path, there is nothing to be grasped.
For this reason, the Path and the element of eye-consciousness are not two; they are non-dual.

Regarding the elements of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness, the Path and the element of mind-consciousness are likewise not two distinct realms. Therefore, it is said: "You yourself are the Path."
"Furthermore, elder sister!
To discern and understand the eye is itself the Way.
The eye is fundamentally empty and pure; if one can comprehend that it is naturally empty, that is the Way."

The ear, nose, mouth, body, and mind are likewise thus: they are fundamentally and spontaneously empty. To awaken to, comprehend, and discern that which is fundamentally pure and spontaneously empty is itself the Way.
The eye is naturally empty; thus, there is no defilement and no resentment. When one perceives no longer being deceived or oppressed, and eliminates lust, anger, and delusion, this is the Way.

The ear, nose, mouth, body, and mind are likewise thus. The mind is naturally so; that which is natural is unstained and free from resentment. When one is not seen to be deceived and eliminates lust, anger, and delusion, that is the Way.
The eye has no master, thus it has no self and nothing that is received;
the Way likewise has no master, thus it has no self and nothing that is received.
It is the same for the ear, nose, mouth, body, and mind: they have no master, no self, and nothing that is received.
The Way also has no master, and thus there is no self, nor is there anything received.
Furthermore, when one calculates the eye, there is neither the dharma of a man nor the dharma of a woman.
Having already understood the Way, there are no dharmas of male or female; being without male and without female is itself the Way.
The ear, nose, mouth, body, and mind likewise have neither male-nature nor female-nature;
the Way is also thus, having neither male nor female.
The Tathāgata has awakened to the fact that visual form and consciousness are without origin; to realize their lack of origin is itself the Way.
The ear, nose, mouth, body, and mind are also like this; when the Tathāgata realizes that the mind has no fundamental basis, such realization is itself the Way.
Therefore, this statement was made: "You yourself are the Way.
Furthermore, Sister, that which is one's own body is devoid of a self;

it is without a self, without a person, without a life-span, without a soul, without form, without mind, without action, without sensation, without seeing, without hearing, without grasping, without relinquishing, without attainment, and without cognition.

The Way is likewise without self, without person, without life-span, without vitality, without male, without female, without body, and without agency; it is without anything seen, nor is there therein the consciousnesses of form, sound, odor, taste, or tangibility. To restrain all phenomena is what constitutes the Way.

As for your body now, Sister, it is ignorant and simple, lacking wisdom; though it exists in the present, it is like grass, trees, walls, tiles, or stones—consisting of the internal element of earth and the external element of earth.
The Tathāgata, by means of his sagely and penetrating wisdom, thoroughly understands this element of earth and has thereby attained perfect enlightenment.
Therefore, this statement is made: "You yourself are the Path.
Furthermore, Sister, regarding the mind, consciousness, thoughts, and reflections—it is when the mind directs the intellect that these phenomena exist.

There is no going and no coming; the body reaches nowhere, and the teaching arrives nowhere. There are no currents, no sinews, and no bones or joints, nor hair of the head or body. It does not abide in the brain, nor does it abide in the marrow; it does not abide internally, nor does it abide externally, nor does it abide in between, nor is there both internal and external.

The eye does not abide, and the ear, nose, mouth, body, and mind likewise do not abide. It abides nowhere, yet is not non-abiding; it is neither established nor is it apart from establishment. It has no location and no territory, and no direction. It is without form and without visibility;
it is without giving and without receiving, without instigation and without instruction, without remainder and without attachment. Pure, fresh, and pristine, it is luminous.

That mind, consciousness, and awareness are likewise without desire or attachment, and there is no one who is pure; they are free from the reliance upon sensory dust, being pure from the very beginning.
For this reason, being without desire or attachment and having no one who is pure, they are luminously manifest and are without a body.
For this reason, there is neither attachment nor purity.

Thus, sister, the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) are naturally the Way (*mārga*), and the Way is also natural; one should clearly understand and discern these aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
If one is able to eliminate the aggregates (*skandha*), the elements (*dhātu*), and the sense bases (*āyatana*) within one's own person, that is the Way (*mārga*). Why is this so?
Because the Way is free from sorrow and grief, and free from harm; for one whose mind understands this, that itself is the Way.
"To realize that all phenomena are entirely equal is itself the Way.
When Mañjuśrī spoke these words in the Udyāna Garden, five hundred devaputras in the sky all conceived the aspiration for supreme, perfect enlightenment.

Among those men and women, great and small, who followed Suvarṇottamaprabhāśrī, two hundred people within that assembly conceived the mind of the Great Way, and sixty gods and humans attained the pure Dharma-eye, free from dust and defilement.

At that time, the noble daughter Suvarṇottamaprabhāśrī, filled with joy and delight, prostrated herself with her five limbs touching the ground. She bowed her head at the feet of Mañjuśrī, took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Saṅgha, and purified her practice of the Brahma-faring while upholding the five precepts. With a mind that was upright and sincere, she gave rise to the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment, and spoke these words:
"I shall follow the teachings of Your Honor."
Mañjuśrī takes pity on all classes of sentient beings so as not to sever the Buddha’s teaching.
Anyone who resolves to attain the Great Way should likewise act in this manner.

Establishing and instituting the gift of Dharma through the Way, he transforms and enlightens the common people; furthermore, by preaching the sutras and the Dharma, he shall wash away their foul and defiled karmic offenses so that they may attain purity, whereby all dharmas become tranquil and entirely serene.

Contemplating in accordance with reality, one sees that fundamentally there is no difference; yet, relying on the body of greed, one engages in perverted acts. Failing to understand equality, one practices lustful desire for form and color. Desire issues forth from the body, and because of this desire, sentient beings encounter the dust and toil of affliction.

“Mañjuśrī! Just as it is now, all phenomena and non-phenomena are fundamentally pure; it is through delusion that they are caused to arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions, resulting in desire.”
I am indeed able to accomplish the gathering and integration of all dharmas and establish myself in the unsurpassed, true, and correct path. Why is this?

All dust-like desires arise from conceptualization and false pretenses; once one has clearly understood that which is false and pretentious, one is then able to eliminate such false and pretentious matters.
Furthermore, I have heard Mañjuśrī explain the meaning of the teachings, distinguishing how the affairs of sensory desires and attachments are like clouds and mist—naturally devoid of reality.
Desire is like a flash of lightning; it vanishes as soon as it appears.
Desire is like the wind; it examines the beginning and the end yet has nothing upon which to rely.
Desire is like empty space; it transcends all realms.
Desire is like a bubble on the water; it cannot endure for long.
Desire is like a ghost’s transformation within which improper thoughts arise;
desire is like a feverish illness, characterized by delirium and false speech.
Desire has no reality of its own; it arises from the conditions of conceptualization.
Desire is like a bond, for it is due to the reckoning of a self.
Desire has no form, for it is due to attachment to the body.
Desire is like a guest who comes; it does not arise from one's original nature.
Desire is manifested through conceptualization, for it follows the various thoughts of the multitude.
Desire is like a dawn vision, arising from manifold conditions.
Desire has no true origin; it arises from covetous longing.
Desire has no object of knowledge; it arises from that notion of "self" and "other.
That which is produced by desire takes the various aggregates (*skandhas*) as its cause.
The realm of desire is like a forge, arising through the mental objects of the sense-spheres.
Desire is like the aggregates (*skandha*), for it employs the sense bases (*āyatana*).
Desire is like a shadow, being a mere designation based on form and name (*nāmarūpa*).
Desire lacks clear comprehension, for it contradicts right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*).
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
Regarding desire, if one can awaken to and comprehend the phrase 'weariness and exhaustion,' then one can know the Way. Why is this so? "
The Way is without movement or change, yet sentient beings are subject to the afflictions of dust and toil.
Desire is like destruction because it discriminates against the Way.
Desire is the mind, for it is the mind that brings about awakening and comprehension.
Desire is like a lute or a zither; it is because one understands it thoroughly. Why is this so?
There is the principle of the Way which does not destroy the dust of desire; because it does not destroy it, one thereby accords with the Way.
If one perceives desire, it is itself the Way. Why is this so?
Because desire enters all realms, reaching everywhere without exception.
If even the Buddha-vehicle is non-existent and lacks form, then the desires of worldly affliction are likewise without form or image.
To seek within all states of existence that which is non-existent and to dwell in non-dwelling—once this has been initiated, it immediately ceases.
The mind is thus natural, and the afflictions are likewise so. Why is this?
Because the mind cannot be scrutinized.
Who says that it can cause the mind to be bound by defilement and delusion?
If that mind cannot be perceived, then sensory desires are likewise invisible; they have no place of accumulation and possess no spatial dimensions.

If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva can thoroughly understand the dharmas of worldly afflictions, they shall teach and transform those who are greedy with the Dharma without weariness; and if they instruct those who are foolish, wrathful, or of equal proportions [of defilements], they shall guide them with the Dharma without becoming indolent or weary.
"Suppose, Mañjuśrī! Just as my own body has desire, so too it is with all those who possess lustful desires.
Just as I have anger and delusion, so too it is with all matters of anger and delusion."
As is my own affliction, so too are the afflictions of all sentient beings.
Just as a great fire completely burns up grasses and trees, the fire of the wisdom of the noble ones burns away and eliminates affliction.
For example, just as the light of the sun illuminates all darkness yet does not mingle with it;
so too is noble wisdom: it eliminates the afflictions of worldly toil yet does not coalesce with them.
For example, just as the wind moves, yet does not cling to any mountains or trees; [so too is noble wisdom].
The Bodhisattva who practices wisdom is likewise: he does not cling to any of the desires of worldly afflictions.
Just as at the end of a kalpa, fire burns all material forms but does not burn empty space;
so too the Bodhisattva who practices wisdom burns away all cravings and desires, yet does not become joined with any worldly afflictions.
Just as pure water does not mix with filth,
so too the bodhisattva does not coexist with worldly dust.
Just as space sustains the earth;
Wisdom is thus not mixed with desire.
Just as a great wind destroys Mount Cakravāḍa,
so too does the bodhisattva, by means of the activity of wisdom, blow away all desires.
It is like the elephant named Jvālāgandha; when milk and water are mixed together, they become of one kind.
In the same way, the Bodhisattva, by means of noble wisdom, wanders through and eliminates the afflictions, transforming them so that they merge with clear insight into a single wisdom.
For example, it is like one who dwells in the northern region beneath Mount Sumeru with his kinsmen, remaining free from negligence and practicing self-discrimination beneath the trees;
so too is the Bodhisattva, whose brilliant wisdom perceives the faculties of sentient beings and discriminates for them accordingly.
“Mañjuśrī! My body, as it is now, does not fear the dust of desire, nor does it find it difficult. Why is this?

Because I understand that the dust of desire is fundamentally and entirely pure, I have donned the armor of the Bodhisattvas of great virtue; thus, with courageous diligence, I encounter no obstacles or difficulties.
For example, one who is a coward seeking a savior is not considered brave;
likewise, a Mahāsattva Bodhisattva is the same—if one is separated from desire, they are not a Bodhisattva.
For example, just as one who is ruined by bandits cannot be considered a valiant general;
so it is with the bodhisattva: one who ruins themselves through craving and desire cannot be considered a bodhisattva.
For example, if a person places a clear-water mani-jewel into a turbid river, it immediately becomes clear and is not defiled by the silt and murkiness.
"In this way, a bodhisattva, while remaining amidst the afflictions of desire and passion, is not defiled by their impurities. At that time,
having spoken these words of praise, Suvarṇottamaprabhāśrī again asked Mañjuśrī,
"What is meant by a bodhisattva being without afflictions?"
He replied:
"If a bodhisattva perceives the arising of thought or perceives the cessation of thought, they should not be called a bodhisattva.
It is like one who has limits; if they behold dhāraṇī, they should not be said to have attained the immeasurable."
Thus, if a bodhisattva perceives the arising and ceasing of the mind within afflictions (*kleśa*), this is not what is meant by a bodhisattva being "free from dust.

One who is free from desire does not perceive the existence of dust nor perceive fetters and resentment; being without seeing or non-seeing, and having distanced oneself from conceptualization (*saṃjñā*), this is called being "free from dust."
Suppose a practitioner attains mastery over their mind, consciousness, and intellect; then regarding all that exists, they will have no notion of nirvana.
Why is this? Because when the mind is free from the conditions of desire, defilement, and conceptual thought, one immediately attains self-mastery.
Regarding all that is good and evil, it is likewise so; he knows all—whether practiced or unpracticed, conditioned or unconditioned, with form or without form.

Regarding the remaining defilements of the dust of birth and death—when the eyes observe forms, the ears hear sounds, the nose perceives fragrances, the tongue tastes flavors, the body experiences touch, and the mind engages with phenomena—if one attains concentration and the will dwells in tranquility, then one is free from the filth of the dust of craving and desire; this is what is called being without negligence, and is designated as being without karma and nothing further to practice. This is precisely what is meant.
One who is free from afflictions is detached from both the conditioned and the unconditioned; thus, they are without blemish.
Furthermore, Sister!
If a bodhisattva’s body is free from afflictions, they are able to deliver others from the defilements of desire; the Tathāgata calls this being free from afflictions.
"To rescue others from the desires of worldly affliction and to practice as a bodhisattva is what constitutes diligence.
The woman asked again,
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s present and immediate diligence?"
Mañjuśrī replied:
“Observing emptiness and non-existence without regressing, one arouses great compassion for sentient beings with false views.
Observing signlessness without regressing, one brings relief through pity for sentient beings who perceive signs.”
He contemplates wishlessness without regressing, and when sentient beings crave wishes, he rescues them with compassion.
He contemplates non-action without regressing, and when sentient beings cling to action, he rescues them with compassion.
Observing that there is nothing produced, one does not regress; yet for the sake of sentient beings in birth and death, one provides compassionate succor.
Observing that there is nothing arisen, one does not regress; yet for the sake of sentient beings in arising and ceasing, one provides compassionate succor.
Contemplating the Śrāvaka vehicle, one attains the fruit of a śrāvaka so as not to regress;
contemplating the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, one attains the fruit of a pratyekabuddha so as not to regress;
contemplating the Bodhisattva vehicle, one does so out of compassion for all sentient beings—this is the bodhisattva’s practice of equanimity and the performance of diligence.
It is, for example, like a man who enters the great ocean and, advancing ever further until he has gone very far, finally reaches a multitude of treasures.
In the same way, Sister!

One should correctly and truthfully observe emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and non-action; one should not give rise to or produce the vehicle of the śrāvakas or the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, but cause those who find progress difficult to reach the stage of non-retrogression, thereby departing from causes and conditions.

Furthermore, sister, it is like someone entering the midst of a great battle; to protect one who is difficult to advance against and to ensure they are not harmed amidst the rage and strife is itself a difficult task.
Such, sister, is this matter!
"One who observes the three gates of liberation with true discernment does not lose skillful means; their difficulty is likewise so.
The girl asked again, "What is meant by a bodhisattva’s skillful means?"
Mañjuśrī replied:
"Skillful means consists in knowing the proper timing and not abandoning those who are terrified by the divisions of birth and death, nor those who cling to the faction of nirvāṇa."

As for provisional skillful means, they manifest the gate of fear, namely: the gate of birth and death; the gate of *nirvāṇa*; the gate of emptiness and non-existence; the gate of what is perceived; the gate of signlessness (*animitta*); the gate of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*); the gate of that which is conceptualized by others; the gate of non-action; the gate of practicing the fundamental virtues of diligence; the gate of non-emergence; the gate of the present world; the gate of non-abiding; the gate of the non-arising of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*); the gate of non-extinction; the gate of the conduct of the scriptures; the gate of tranquility; the gate of opening and transforming sentient beings through guidance; the gate of the *dharmadhātu*; the gate of protecting the true Dharma; the gate of the *śrāvaka*; the gate of the *pratyekabuddha*; the gate of expounding the Buddha-way; and the gate of crossing over via the Buddha-way.
If a bodhisattva perceives the gate of fear, yet remains unattached to any gate whatsoever, this is called skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
To state the essential point:
it is the gate of desire, for it is free from all craving.
The gate of anger is that which is free from resentment;
the gate of folly is that which is free from ignorance;
the gate of affliction is that which is free from defilement.
It is the gateway of all realms of existence (*gati*), for there is no coming or going; this is the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of a bodhisattva.

As for the gateways of the practices of all foolish commoners, those in training (*śaikṣa*), those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas—one who is able to clearly understand these various gateways is said to possess skillful means.
At that time, the World-Honored One was walking up and down by a spring on Vulture Peak Mountain, accompanied by the Venerable Ānanda as his attendant.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One praised him from afar:
"Excellent, excellent!"

Mañjuśrī! This is the bodhisattva’s practice of diligence through skillful means, cultivated and applied in the present before one's eyes; it is exactly as you have described, equal and without distinction.

At that moment, by means of this sound of "Excellent! (*sādhu*), it was immediately proclaimed throughout the trichiliocosm; its resonance pervaded everywhere, causing the earth to quake in six ways. Then, countless devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings—hearing the sound of "Excellent!", all received the command and proceeded to the Buddha’s dwelling. Prostrating at his feet, they withdrew to stand to one side and each addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Great Sage, what did you praise just now, such that the entire trichiliocosm has been notified and the great thousandfold world-system has quaked in six ways?"
The World-Honored One replied,
"If the Devaputra wishes to know, it is because Mañjuśrī has exhorted and transformed others.
He asked again:
"Where have you been wandering now?
The Buddha said,
"At the foot of the eastern gate of Rājagṛha, on the main street, I was extensively expounding the Dharma and discussing the ultimate goal for Suvarṇaprabhāsottama."
"O Son of Heaven!
You all should go and seek the meaning of the Dharma.

At that time, the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings—all together, in unison—went to the place where Mañjuśrī was speaking. They manifested half their bodies and rained down celestial flowers, which completely covered the great city of Rājagṛha.
At that time, the devas saw humans and humans saw the devas; each dwelt in peace and security, free from contention.
Furthermore, countless thousands of people in the city of Rājagṛha each took the flowers scattered by the devas and brought them to Mañjuśrī.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru, together with the fourfold army, the ladies of the harem and court attendants, the ministers and officials, and all the subordinate kings, went forth as one to visit Mañjuśrī.

Furthermore, when the venerable elders, the sons of householders, the crown princes, and the ministers beheld the majestic splendor of Suvarṇaprabhāsaśrī’s deportment, his faculties serene and tranquil, having destroyed worldly afflictions and abandoned all perversions, and seeing himself thus adorned with sublime virtues, they no longer gave rise to thoughts of desire.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed Suvarṇottamaprabhāśrī:
"Now that this great assembly has gathered here, for what reason are they no longer subject to defiled attachment?"
"Where now are those sensual desires previously craved?
The woman replied to Mañjuśrī:
"The defiled desires of all sentient beings establish the resolve for wisdom and liberation at the primordial limit (koṭi), abiding in the dharma-realm, which is a place without origin."
The Unoriginated is thus, without distinction; it is without birth, without cessation, and has no location.
Furthermore, those sensory desires are inherently pure, being the differentiation of equality.
He asked the woman again,
"What is meant by 'defilements and desires being fundamentally pure'?
She replied:
“Without perception or non-perception, without response or non-response, these sensory desires are fundamentally pure;
since sensory objects arise from compliant conduct yet do not originate, they are fundamentally pure.”

One should know that sensory desires come as transient visitors; one should clearly realize that the wisdom of emptiness dwells together with the Path. The wisdom of signlessness, the wisdom of wishlessness, and the luminosity of original purity all dwell together, observing that all these things are entirely non-existent.

It is like a venomous serpent that harbors poison to harm others; yet if someone comes bringing excellent medicine capable of neutralizing its poisonous wrath, as soon as the serpent sees this medicine, its venom is immediately extinguished.

When people—whether men or women, young or old—realize the poison has been entirely eliminated, they all play with it together, placing it upon their laps and knees; it causes no injury and does not bite anyone.

Such a person, when they had not yet heard the Dharma and Vinaya, dwelt upon what was improper; their views were inverted, and being situated amidst the dust of desire, they were consumed by it, their own bodies possessed by greed and attached to outward appearances.

Having already been able to contemplate that form is like a mass of foam, one then knows that the phenomena of the body are like magical illusions, and that the play of conceptual discrimination is like a dream.
Having understood that craving and desire are like water bubbles, that life is like morning dew, and that all things are impermanent.
He clearly understands that all the aggregates (*skandha*) are equally afflictive and distressing; he knows the body is impure and entirely empty and non-existent.

He contemplates that all phenomena (*dharma*) are devoid of self, and through correct and thorough reflection, he realizes that both their origin and end are utterly void. He does not disparage others nor praise himself; he neither binds himself nor binds others.
Now, having heard the Dharma taught by you, I immediately believed and rejoiced, thereby attaining liberation; for this reason, my vision is free from any defilement or attachment. Why is this so?
“Reflecting on the teaching of benevolence, one responds to what arises and dwells amidst the defilements; calculating the defilements in this way, there is no stain of desire.
Who then could perceive them? At that time, Śreṣṭhadhvaja addressed Mañjuśrī:

“The entire great assembly of devas and humans may well feel fear. Pray, analyze and expound the Dharma as is appropriate, so that these devas and humans may understand that the root of worldly desires is entirely pure. Out of compassion for all, cause them to resolve upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.”
Mañjuśrī replied: "The sensory dusts are fundamentally pure, yet those who have faith and delight in this are rare. Why is this so?"
This is because of non-awakening.
When one awakens to the purity of sensory objects (*viṣaya*), one attains the Way.
It is like a fire that has not yet arisen, which cannot burn a person.
Thus you should know:
when there is no thought of ideation, one does not act with the notion of "I" or "mine";
it is like a fire that has been kindled which turns back to burn itself.
Thus one should know:
the thoughts of conceptualization and the afflictions of craving create the body of birth and death;
it is like wood producing fire, whose flames then grow ever more intense.
Thus you should know:
when false views and perversions arise, the afflictions (kleśa) cause the three realms to blaze;
yet, once the fire is extinguished, there is no longer any flame or light.
Thus you should know:
when inverted views have ceased, defilements do not arise; consequently, one does not give rise to the dust of toil within the triple world.
It is like a fire that has been extinguished for hundreds of thousands of years and no longer burns; people harbor no doubt, fear, or dread regarding the cold ashes.
Thus one should know:
although one may have practiced amidst the defilements of sensual desire for many kalpas, once one has understood and contemplated them, there is nothing accumulated;
like a fire that has been extinguished and can no longer be used, when the light of wisdom is serene and tranquil, the afflictions of worldly toil do not arise.
Just as the fire within the body, though its heat and warmth may be intense,
does not burn anything, so too should one reckon it:
although adventitious dusts and desires may arise, they ultimately cannot defile the source-limit of the mind, which is fundamentally pure and radiantly luminous.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī again asked the girl,
"Furthermore, how should one contemplate the physical body?
She replied:
"It is like the reflection of the moon in water.
He asked again:
"How does one contemplate the essence of the five aggregates?"
He replied,
"It is just like the emanation of a Tathāgata who has passed into parinirvāṇa.
He asked again:
"How should the various elements be contemplated? He replied:
"They are like the two elements of water and fire."
He asked again:
"How does one contemplate the phenomena of the sense bases?
He replied:
"It is like the practice of neither sin nor merit, being devoid of the causal conditions of giving.
He asked again:
"How does one contemplate these assemblies?"
He replied:
"It illuminates the nature and mind of all those gathered in the assembly.
He asked again:
“How does one further contemplate that body?
He replied, “It is just like my own parents; for one in the state of equanimity, there is no duality.”
He asked again:
"How does one contemplate my body?
He replied:
"It is just like one born blind who cannot see any forms.
He asked again:
"How have you ever heard this Dharma?"
He replied,
"I have heard this Dharma as one who hears it when a magician conjures a conjured person.
He asked again:
"How is it that you have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment?
He replied:
"I am this very path; there is nothing to be sought after."
He asked again:
"What is meant by practicing the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā)?
He replied:
"To cultivate all the perfections (pāramitās) is to abandon all worldly defilements.
He asked again:
"Is it for the sake of fulfilling the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā)?"
He replied,
"That which is fully possessed is as all-pervasive and complete as space.
He asked again:
"Is it for the sake of practicing patience?
He replied,
"It is to cultivate all dharmas as being without arising and without birth."
He asked again,
“Are you practicing with diligent and energetic perseverance?
He replied:
"One practices all dharmas without reaching any point of convergence.
He asked again:
"Is this the establishment of the perfection of tranquility (śamatha-pāramitā)?"
He replied:
"It is established within the dharma-realm, abiding in non-abiding.
He asked again:
"Is it that one has already fulfilled the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)?
He replied:
"It is that one's resolve is free from arrogance and the mind does not consider itself superior."
He asked again:
"Do you practice loving-kindness?
He replied:
"Because he considers that all sentient beings are entirely non-existent.
He asked again:
"Where should one seek the Bodhisattva Mahākāruṇika?"
He replied:
"One should seek it within the afflictions of sentient beings. Why is this so?"
“The Bodhisattva Mahākaruṇā, wishing to control the afflictions of sentient beings, then gives rise to the aspiration for unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment.
He asked again:
“What should the Bodhisattva Pramuditā seek?”
He replied:
"The truthfulness of one's own mind, the purity of one's disposition, and the transformation of all sorrows and griefs—this is the joy of a bodhisattva.
He asked again:
“Regarding the Bodhisattva’s practice of protection, how is it fulfilled?
He replied:
“Whatever matters of contention, conflict, or strife arise among sentient beings, he fulfills his task by transforming them so that they reach a state of peace and harmony.”
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'contention'?
He replied:
"He is one who eliminates unreal and false afflictions, and whose resolve is established in the Buddha-way.
He asked again:
"With whom does he contend?"
He replied,
"It is because my mind does not accord with that of the various heterodox teachers outside [the Buddhist fold].
He asked again:
“What constitutes the various heterodox and deviant teachings?
He replied, “It is those who,
seeing what others have initiated, are unable to practice forbearance and instead follow their own impulses.”
He asked again:
"To what does the bodhisattva’s patience aspire?
He replied:
"It is for the sake of transforming and enlightening all sentient beings.
Why is this so? If one does not guide and lead them, how can one be said to transform sentient beings through the practice of patience?"
"To be without anger, resentment, or sorrowful distress is what constitutes patience.
He asked again,
"What is meant by 'harm'?"
He replied,
"To accumulate roots of virtue for the sake of things that cause distress and affliction is itself a peril.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'harmlessness'?
He replied:
"When the various realms are free from anxiety, one maintains benevolence; this is what is called harmlessness."
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'the bodhisattva’s battle of selection'?
He replied:
"Because when one selects all dharmas, nothing is obtained.
He asked again:
"How does a bodhisattva subdue the various māras?"
He replied:
"Because there is no attachment, one does not extinguish the afflictions. Why is this so?
The Bodhisattva subdues the five aggregates and does not dwell together with the sensory dusts; by this, he triumphs over Māra.

The Bodhisattva subdues the dusts yet is not defiled by them, for he has fundamentally understood all phenomena from beginning to end. He transforms and enlightens sentient beings, eliminating the afflictions of old age and death.
He addressed the devaputras, saying:
"The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī has already transcended all notions of omniscience, the supernormal powers, and wisdom.
He then asked the girl:
“How does a bodhisattva transform and enlighten sentient beings?
He replied:
“By single-mindedly wielding skillful means and practicing wisdom.”
He asked again:
"How does a bodhisattva establish all sentient beings?
He replied:
“Only when a Bodhisattva has established the wisdom of their own mind and attained sage-like penetration can they transform and enlighten all sentient beings.
He asked again,
“Now that you have preached the Dharma, this entire assembly has listened and received it well.”
He replied:
"This is not one who listens and receives well. Why is that? Because—"
"Because one still harbors the notion of 'self' and 'others,' yet conversely encourages others, it is because one remains established in consciousness.
He asked again:
"What is meant by hearing the Dharma as a true listener?"
He replied:

"If one can believe that oneself is like a dream, and that the preaching of the Dharma is like a magician’s conjuration, perceiving the listening as a provisional sound, neither clinging to that voice nor constructing a conceptual liberation—possessing these two qualities, this is what is called 'skillfully hearing and receiving the Dharma.'"
He asked again:
"How does one listen to and receive the principles of the Dharma?
He replied:
“Mañjuśrī is one who takes refuge in the Dharma.

At that time, Suvarṇottamaprabhāśrī, empowered by the majestic spiritual authority established by the youth Mañjuśrī and through the wisdom cultivated by her own fundamental virtues, preached the Dharma appropriately within the assembly.
Twelve thousand people all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path.
Five hundred devaputras, who had planted roots of virtue in the past and were intent upon the Bodhisattva vehicle, attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Thirty-two thousand devas and humans distanced themselves from and were freed from the dust and defilements of all phenomena, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.

Having finished preaching the Dharma, the woman felt joy in her heart and immediately attained the *anulomikī-dharmakṣānti* (receptive patience in accordance with the Dharma). She then cast herself at the feet of Mañjuśrī to take refuge, saying:
"I pray that the Most Holy One will allow my body to become a śramaṇa. May you show compassion and deliver me from these non-conforming thoughts; the conduct of the multitude is not a noble vision."
At that time, Mañjuśrī said:
"A bodhisattva does not consider the shaving of one's own hair to be true renunciation. Why is this so?
To be able to sever and extinguish the desires and defilements of sentient beings, causing them to cultivate diligence—this is the renunciation of a bodhisattva.
A bodhisattva does not consider merely wearing the *kāṣāya* to be renunciation.

As for the name of the *kāṣāya*, in the Jin language it is called "removing impurity"; it should remove the stains of lust, anger, and ignorance from sentient beings, ensuring they are free from blemish and constantly practice diligence—this is the renunciation of a bodhisattva.
A bodhisattva does not consider the personal observance of precepts to be true renunciation;
rather, it is the transformation of sentient beings so that they observe caution and restraint that constitutes the renunciation of a bodhisattva.
A bodhisattva does not consider dwelling in seclusion for oneself to be true renunciation;
rather, even if one follows the various classes of beings throughout the five destinies, being able to establish the seclusion of wisdom therein is the true renunciation of a bodhisattva.
A bodhisattva does not consider physical appearance, demeanor, or ritual decorum to be true renunciation;
rather, transforming the common people and encouraging them to establish compassion is the true renunciation of a bodhisattva.
A bodhisattva does not consider the cultivation of his own merit to be true renunciation;
rather, it is the exhortation and manifestation that causes all sentient beings to flourish and plant the roots of virtue that constitutes the renunciation of a bodhisattva.
A bodhisattva does not consider it to be renunciation merely to seek their own liberation through personal extinction;
rather, to liberate the minds of all sentient beings and lead them to extinction is truly the renunciation of a bodhisattva.
A bodhisattva does not consider the removal of their own afflictions to be renunciation;
rather, the eradication of the afflictions of all sentient beings is what constitutes the renunciation of a bodhisattva.
A bodhisattva does not consider it to be renunciation merely to protect one's own person or to guard one's own mind alone;
rather, to protect the aspirations and minds of all sentient beings is the true renunciation of a bodhisattva.
A bodhisattva does not consider personal liberation alone to be true renunciation;
rather, it is the deliverance of all sentient beings from the cycle of birth and death that constitutes the renunciation of a bodhisattva.
A bodhisattva does not consider the mere rescue of oneself from the afflictions of birth and death to be true renunciation;
rather, it is the liberation of all beings from the afflictions of birth and death that constitutes the renunciation of a bodhisattva.
A bodhisattva does not consider the aspiration for nirvana to be true renunciation;

rather, it is the complete fulfillment of all the dharmas of the Buddhas that constitutes the renunciation of a bodhisattva. Furthermore, it is characterized by great compassion in rescuing sentient beings, not seeing the faults of others, not speaking of their deficiencies, praising the virtue of those who possess firm faith, and manifesting faithful practice to bestow it upon all—this is what is meant.
"Those who have left the household life rely upon others, whereas those who are bodhisattvas have nothing upon which to rely.
The girl asked Mañjuśrī,
"What is meant by 'leaving the household life while relying upon others'?"
He then replied to the woman:
"One who has left the household life relies upon the prohibitive precepts, yet does not consider the mere observance of precepts to be leaving the household life.

If you wish to know it, O woman, set your will upon meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), let your mind be free from negligence, rely on wisdom when leaving the household life rather than following evil companions, and practice the gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*); this is what constitutes leaving the household life."
"If the mind is not yet liberated, one does not truly leave the household life.
He asked again:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva not relying on others?"
He replied:
"If one does not place faith in another person, then there is no dependence; nor does one observe the facial expressions of others to inquire:
'What wisdom do they possess from which I might receive enlightenment?'"
What extraordinary virtues do those people possess?
They shall attain the various supernormal powers and great wisdom;
yet they harbor no expectations regarding their own persons.
"This is what is called not relying on others.
When Mañjuśrī spoke this Chapter on Leaving Home, five hundred bodhisattvas each removed their robes, precious jewels, and necklaces, and together offered them all to Mañjuśrī, saying these words:
"Having heard the Honored One’s excellent teaching on leaving home, we too shall follow this righteous principle and practice accordingly, fulfilling the path of renunciation."
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī said to Śikharadhara:

"If you were to return once more on a carriage drawn by superior thoroughbred horses and, together with the householder’s son Bhayadatta, preach this for the sake of transforming and instructing him, that would be your practice of renunciation."
At that time, each person in the great assembly thought to themselves:
"How can one who is free from desire dwell together with those who possess desire?
The woman immediately perceived the thoughts in the minds of the assembly and replied to them, explaining the matter for their benefit:
“A bodhisattva who is free from desire is born together with those beings who possess desire, desiring to transform and enlighten them so that they may become pure.

You should know that when a bodhisattva is free from hatred and delusion, he is born and dwells together with the multitudes who possess hatred and delusion, desiring to transform and enlighten them by bestowing compassion and wisdom.”

Suppose a bodhisattva, having already departed from worldly afflictions, is born together with those sentient beings who are driven by desire, in order to transform and guide all those who are dissolute.
This is like a person where mother and child dwell together without being defiled;
so it is with the bodhisattva, who constantly associates with all sentient beings without being defiled.
It is like a lute player or a master of divine incantations who, though practicing what they desire, remains free from desire;
so it is with the Bodhisattva, who dwells amidst the perceptions of the triple world yet, like a divine incantation or art, remains unstained by attachment.

At that time, Suvarṇottamaprabhāśrī attained the opportune moment and realized the meaning of the Dharma; reaching the light that leaves behind all darkness, she beheld the afflictions and was revealed to the True Truth. She then stepped forward, prostrated at the feet of Mañjuśrī, circumambulated him three times, returned to her carriage, and spoke these verses:
"The fundamental nature is pure, And desire cannot defile it.
Therein is no anger, For one always cultivates a heart of loving-kindness."
Nor was there any ignorance; he gave rise to the light of wisdom.
With such supreme virtue, he then mounted his chariot.
Previously, following the son of Bimbasāra, he had practiced heedlessness.
My mind was once driven by greed and desire; now it has found its refuge.
Amidst all fears and hardships, it is the craving for wealth and profit that causes them.
Having mounted this vehicle to depart from these things, I raise my voice to sing this hymn of praise.
Just as when thick, heavy clouds rain down and moisten the earth,
they obscure the palace of the sun, so that people cannot see it with their eyes;
yet its radiance does not become darkened, nor is there anyone who can seize its light.
Just as adventitious clouds prevent light from appearing,
so too is the mind of the fool inherently pure;
yet adventitious defilements likewise obscure the light of wisdom through the failure to realize the nature of conceptualization.
Those who are reckoned as enlightened do not abide in any location;
having already eliminated all afflictions, they are designated as "possessing wisdom.
Their wisdom is free from arrogance, and their minds are pure and undiminished.
When pushed back, it comes from nowhere; when sent forth, it goes nowhere.
If one’s thoughts do not accord with the Right, then there will be defilements and desires;
once one has responded with thoughts in accordance with the Dharma, one proceeds toward the state of non-attainment.
That which is called "name" has no location, and there is no one who receives it;
thus, there is nothing that arises, nor is there anything that ceases.
There is no giving and nothing to be relinquished, nor does one rely upon another.
How joyful is this True Dharma, subtle, wondrous, and exceedingly pure!
Like an oil-fed lamp that illuminates all depths of darkness,
those who dwell in ignorance and obscurity do not know where to turn for refuge.
Wisdom is likewise so: it extinguishes all ignorance and darkness;
seeing no place for worldly afflictions, one follows mindfulness to fulfill the purpose of one's coming.
It is like a skilled physician who treats all manner of diseases.
The body neither increases nor decreases, and there is nothing lost or forgotten.
Illness is but a transient guest; once its affliction has been extinguished, there is no further habitual tendency, for one knows not the destination where the ailment has departed.
Samantabhadra is likewise: with his most gentle voice, he beholds the calamities and ailments of sentient beings and treats them in various ways;
he removes defilements to bring about purity and leads them toward the gateway of wisdom.
